emphasis: Enzymes are generally heat-labile proteins; heating disrupts the structure needed for catalysis

rationales.a: Stereospecificity is characteristic of enzymes because a structured active site selectively binds substrate stereoisomers.
rationales.b: An enzyme can cycle through catalytic states, but it is regenerated at the end rather than consumed as a reactant.
rationales.c: Most enzymes are proteins, although catalytic RNA molecules (ribozymes) are exceptions.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q002.takeaway: Enzymes accelerate reactions by lowering activation energy, not by raising the barrier.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q002.displayText:
Enzymes accelerate reactions by lowering activation energy, not by raising the barrier.

Enzymes do not catalyze a reaction by increasing the activation energy, rather they do it by
decreasing the activation energy.

Specific acid or base catalysis, catalysis by proximity, catalysis by strain all constitute mechanisms
of enzyme to enhance the rate of reaction.

Enzymes use combinations of four general mechanisms to achieve enhancements of the rates of
chemical reactions:
• Covalent catalysis
• Specific acid or base catalysis
• Catalysis by proximity
• Catalysis by strain
emphasis: Enzymes accelerate reactions by lowering activation energy, not by raising the barrier

rationales.a: Proximity catalysis increases effective local reactant concentration and favors productive encounters.
rationales.b: Acid–base catalysis uses proton donation or acceptance to stabilize reaction intermediates or facilitate bond changes.
rationales.c: Strain catalysis distorts substrate geometry toward a transition state, reducing the energetic barrier.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 283; explanation p. 289.

emphasis: Mitochondrial superoxide dismutase is the manganese-dependent isoform; cytosolic SOD is Cu/Zn-dependent

rationales.c: Tyrosinase is a copper-dependent oxidase involved in melanin synthesis.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q006.displayText:
A metal loosely associated with an enzyme is a metal-activated cofactor; tightly bound metal characterizes a metalloenzyme.

Enzymes that. use’metal-ion asia Cofactor are termed as metal-activated enzymes (and
not metalloenzymes). ©
Metalloenzymes are prosthetic groups in which the metal is tightly and irreversibly bound to the
enzyme. The metal forms an integral part of its active structure. Metal-activated enzymes are
those that have a cofactor containing metal (inorganic) which are loosely and reversibly bound to

the enzyme. They show enhanced activity in the addition of metal.

A cofactor is a non-protein part of a holoenzyme that can be separated part from the protein part.
Cofactors are mostly metal ions or inorganic. If an organic compound is present in a cofactor, it is
called a coenzyme. Cofactors serve functions similar to those of prosthetic groups. Cofactors bind
in a transient, dissociable manner to enzymes. Cofactors must be present in the medium
surrounding the enzyme for catalysis to occur.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q011.takeaway: Ligases join two molecules, typically coupling bond formation to ATP or another nucleoside-triphosphate hydrolysis.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q011.displayText:
Ligases join two molecules, typically coupling bond formation to ATP or another nucleoside-triphosphate hydrolysis.

The group of enzymes that catalyze the joining together of two molecules with the hydrolysis of
ATP is called ligases.
emphasis: Ligases join two molecules, typically coupling bond formation to ATP or another nucleoside-triphosphate hydrolysis

rationales.a: Transferases move a functional group between molecules; they do not define ATP-coupled joining of two substrates.
rationales.c: Oxidoreductases transfer electrons or hydrogen atoms rather than joining two molecules through a new bond.
rationales.d: Lyases add or remove groups to form double bonds or cleave bonds without hydrolysis; they are not the ATP-dependent joining class.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q012.takeaway: Lipoprotein lipase has a physiological role in plasma; LDH, ALP and GGT are commonly treated as nonfunctional plasma enzymes/clinical markers.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q012.displayText:
Lipoprotein lipase has a physiological role in plasma; LDH, ALP and GGT are commonly treated as nonfunctional plasma enzymes/clinical markers.

Lipoprotein lipase is not a non-functional enzyme. It is a functional enzyme.

Functional enzymes have a specific function in the plasma such as coagulation factors,
pseudocholinesterases, and lipoprotein lipases.

Nonfunctional enzymes have no specific function in the plasma.
• They are released from the cells as a result of normal wear and tear. Their level is very low in
serum.
• They serve as biomarkers whose levels in the plasma can assist in the diagnosis and prognosis of
diseases affecting specific tissues.
• Eg: Lactate dehydrogenase, Creatine kinase, alkaline phosphatase, gamma glutamyl
transpeptidase.

. Oo
emphasis: Lipoprotein lipase has a physiological role in plasma; LDH, ALP and GGT are commonly treated as nonfunctional plasma enzymes/clinical markers

rationales.b: Alkaline phosphatase in serum is commonly interpreted as a tissue-release marker, especially in cholestatic or bone disease.
rationales.c: Lactate dehydrogenase is present in tissues and enters plasma with cell turnover or injury, where it serves as a marker.
rationales.d: Gamma-glutamyl transferase is a membrane enzyme whose serum activity is used as a marker, including in hepatobiliary disease.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q016.takeaway: ALT is more liver-specific than AST in acute viral hepatocellular injury because ALT is concentrated in hepatocytes.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q016.displayText:
ALT is more liver-specific than AST in acute viral hepatocellular injury because ALT is concentrated in hepatocytes.

The enzyme most specific for his condition, acute viral hepatitis, is alanine aminotransferase
(ALT).

Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is predominantly found in the liver and therefore is a more
specific marker for hepatocellular damage than AST.

Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) is found in various tissues. The AST/ALT ratio is very
important.
• AST/ALT <1 is seen in hepatocellular damage like in NAFLD, toxic hepatitis, paracetamol
toxicity. In cirrhosis, the ratio becomes more than 1.

• AST/ALT> 2 is suggestive while AST/ALT> 3 is highly suggestive of alcoholic liver disease.
Other options:

Option A: Alkaline phosphatase rise is seen in many liver diseases but more than fourfold rise
indicates cholestasis.

Option D: GGT is used to identify occult alcohol use.
emphasis: ALT is more liver-specific than AST in acute viral hepatocellular injury because ALT is concentrated in hepatocytes

rationales.a: ALP is most useful for cholestatic or infiltrative patterns and is not as specific for hepatocellular injury as ALT.
rationales.b: AST is present in liver and extrahepatic tissues, including muscle and heart, making it less liver-specific.
rationales.d: GGT supports hepatobiliary origin of an elevated ALP and can reflect alcohol exposure, but it is not the most specific marker here.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 287; explanation p. 295,296.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q018.takeaway: Elastase prefers small neutral residues such as alanine (and glycine) at the P1 position of its substrate.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q018.displayText:
Elastase prefers small neutral residues such as alanine (and glycine) at the P1 position of its substrate.

Elastase is a serine protease that cleaves at the carboxy-terminal of neutral amino acids like
alanine and glycine.

Serine proteases are proteolytic enzymes having Serine, Histidine and Aspartate at the active
site. The active site consists of two binding sites and a catalytic site. While serine is present in the
catalytic site of serine proteases, histidine and aspartate are present on binding sites.

Serine proteases differ in substrate specificity.
• Trypsin cleaves the carboxy-terminal of basic amino acids like arginine and lysine.
• Chymotrypsin cleaves at the carboxy-terminal of bulky hydrophobic amino acids like tryptophan,
phenylalanine, and tyrosine.

« Elastase cleaves at the carboxy-terminal of neutral amino acids like alanine and glycine.
emphasis: Elastase prefers small neutral residues such as alanine (and glycine) at the P1 position of its substrate

rationales.a: Arginine is a basic residue preferred by trypsin-like proteases, not the small neutral-residue preference of elastase.
rationales.c: Tryptophan is bulky and aromatic; chymotrypsin favors aromatic residues rather than elastase's small-residue pocket.
rationales.d: Phenylalanine is bulky and aromatic and is a preferred chymotrypsin substrate, not an elastase preference.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 288; explanation p. 296.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q019.takeaway: Aldolase follows a sequential two-substrate mechanism; serine proteases, aminotransferases and pyruvate carboxylase are classic ping-pong examples.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH18_Q019.displayText:
Aldolase follows a sequential two-substrate mechanism; serine proteases, aminotransferases and pyruvate carboxylase are classic ping-pong examples.

Aldolase does not participate in a ping-pong reaction. Ping pong reactions are a type of Bi-Bi
reaction.

Bi-Bi reaction is a two substrate two product reaction. Most of the Bi-Bi reactions follow
Michaelis-Menten kinetics. There are three types of Bi-Bi reactions:
• Ordered Bi-Bi reaction: Example- NAD(P)H-dependant oxidoreductases.
• Random Bi-Bi reaction: Example- Most kinases and dehydrogenases.
• Ping pong reaction: Example- Serine proteases, aminotransferases and pyruvate carboxylase.
emphasis: Aldolase follows a sequential two-substrate mechanism; serine proteases, aminotransferases and pyruvate carboxylase are classic ping-pong examples

rationales.a: Many serine proteases form an acyl-enzyme intermediate after the first substrate leaves, a ping-pong pattern.
rationales.b: Aminotransferases transfer an amino group via enzyme-bound pyridoxamine phosphate between successive substrates, consistent with ping-pong kinetics.
rationales.c: Pyruvate carboxylase uses a biotin-bound carboxyl group transferred between sites/substrates in a ping-pong sequence.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 288; explanation p. 297.
